passage: Mohit, you asked why I'm so strict about teasing. Let your Sudha Nani tell you something I've never told your mother. When I was nine, my father shouted every evening. At home I was small, invisible. At school I wanted to be big. There was a girl in my class, Kusum, very quiet, who ate alone and never answered back. I noticed her the way a cat notices a sparrow. She had done nothing to me. Nothing at all. But the other girls laughed when I teased her, and for once people looked at me like I mattered. That's what I wanted, beta. Not to hurt her exactly. To feel strong. It took me many years to understand that.

qa.q: What was the quiet girl's name in Sudha Nani's class?
qa.a: Her name was Kusum.

qa.q: What did Sudha Nani really want when she chose Kusum?
qa.a: She wanted to feel strong and noticed, because at home she felt small and invisible with her father shouting.

qa.q: If an adult had noticed nine-year-old Sudha at this first stage, what could they have done?
qa.a: They could have given her real ways to feel important, like responsibility in class, and paid attention to what was going on at home, while protecting Kusum.

qa.q: How might Kusum have experienced being picked out?
qa.a: She probably felt confused and scared, since she had done nothing and couldn't understand why she was chosen.

grounding: It shows a child who felt powerless at home choosing a quiet classmate as a target to gain status, not because of anything the classmate did.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof and recess was cancelled, so class 4B stayed inside while their teacher was called away. Uday leaned back on his bench. Rupa's friends would tell. Then he saw Harsha, drawing quietly in the corner, alone, shoulders curled. Harsha never argued, even when someone took his crayons. Uday smiled a little. He glanced at the boys near him to make sure they were watching, then stood up and strolled over, slowly, the whole class suddenly quiet.

Teacher's note, Class 4, Monday

Rashmi, her mother tells me, is the youngest of four, and her older sisters decide everything for her. This week she has started standing close to the tallest girls at recess, laughing loudly at their jokes.

Today she noticed Kiran, the new girl who speaks softly and never argues, and watched Kiran not complain when someone stepped on her crayon. Then Rashmi said something to the tall girls, looking at Kiran, and they all laughed.

Kiran had done nothing. I think Rashmi chose her because she seemed safe to pick on, and because the laughter made Rashmi feel big.

I have moved their seats and will talk to Rashmi tomorrow about how she feels at home and here, and check in with Kiran.

— Urmila Ma'am

qa.q: How many children are there in Rashmi's family?
qa.a: Four; she is the youngest.

qa.q: What does Urmila Ma'am think Rashmi wants when she laughs at Kiran with the tall girls?
qa.a: She thinks Rashmi wants to feel big and admired, since at home she has little say.

qa.q: What did Urmila Ma'am do well in response?
qa.a: She noticed early, moved their seats, planned to talk to Rashmi about her feelings, and to check in with Kiran.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel when the tall girls laugh while looking at her?
qa.a: She is likely confused and hurt, not knowing what she did, because she did nothing.

grounding: A teacher's note shows Rashmi, powerless at home, choosing a quiet classmate as a target to gain status, not because of anything the target did.

passage:
Monday

Bhaiya took my cricket bat again and said I was too small to play. Papa just laughed. Nobody listens to me at home.

At school today there's this new boy, Asif. He's really quiet. When Deepak bumped his bag off the desk, Asif just picked it up and said nothing. Didn't even look angry.

I watched him all through maths. Everyone likes it when I make jokes. If I make jokes about Asif, they'll laugh at him and not at me.

At lunch I called him "Mouse" because he's so quiet. Deepak and Nitin laughed so hard. It felt good. Like being big.

Asif didn't say anything. He just went red.

I don't know why I did it. He never did anything to me.

— Vijay

qa.q: What nickname did Vijay give Asif?
qa.a: "Mouse".

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Deepak and Nitin laughed?
qa.a: Vijay felt good and big, the opposite of feeling small and unheard at home.

qa.q: What could an adult do if they read this diary?
qa.a: Talk kindly to Vijay about feeling powerless at home, explain that picking on Asif is not okay, and make sure Asif is supported.

qa.q: What is it like for Asif to be called "Mouse"?
qa.a: He likely feels embarrassed and hurt, going red, and confused since he did nothing.

grounding: Vijay's diary shows a child who feels powerless at home picking a quiet classmate as a target to win laughs and status, not because of anything the target did.

passage:
At the government school in the village near Ambala, Sahil was the one everyone laughed with. But at home, his three older cousins bossed him around and teased him every evening, and nobody listened when he complained.

At recess he watched Mohit, a thin boy from the next village who ate his roti alone under the neem tree and never raised his voice.

Mohit wouldn't fight back. Sahil could tell.

The next day Sahil walked past and flicked Mohit's steel tiffin lid off. It clanged on the ground. The boys around Sahil laughed and looked at him as if he were a hero.

Mohit quietly picked it up.

Sahil laughed too, but somewhere under the laughing he felt like his cousins.

qa.q: Where did Mohit eat his roti alone?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when the boys looked at him like a hero?
qa.a: He felt powerful and admired, but also uneasy, feeling like his cousins.

qa.q: What could a teacher do after noticing this?
qa.a: Talk to Sahil calmly about what is going on for him and why he picked Mohit, stop the behaviour, and check on Mohit.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel picking up the tiffin lid?
qa.a: He probably feels humiliated and alone, not understanding why he was picked.

grounding: Sahil, powerless at home, notices a quiet classmate who won't fight back and targets him for admiration, not because of anything Mohit did.

passage:
At home in Melbourne, Jin's older brothers took the TV remote, the last dumpling and the front seat, every single time. Jin never won.
At school on Monday he watched the new girl, Nadia, drop her pencil case. Two boys stepped on it by accident. She just picked everything up, face red, and said nothing. Jin noticed that. He noticed how she ate lunch in the corner of the library steps, and how she never looked up when someone bumped her.
Something small and hungry woke up in him. Here, maybe, was someone smaller than him.
He grinned at his friends. "Watch this," he said, and walked towards the library steps.

qa.q: What did Nadia do when her pencil case was stepped on?
qa.a: She just picked everything up, face red, and said nothing.

qa.q: What does Jin want when he says 'Watch this' to his friends?
qa.a: He wants to feel powerful and admired for once, since at home he always feels small and never wins.

qa.q: How could a teacher or parent step in at this stage?
qa.a: An adult who notices could keep an eye on Nadia and give Jin real ways to feel strong and respected, before any teasing begins.

qa.q: What would change if Nadia knew why Jin was choosing her?
qa.a: She might see that it was about Jin's need to feel bigger, not about anything she did, which could ease any shame she felt.

grounding: Shows a child who feels powerless at home picking a quiet classmate who doesn't fight back, out of his own need for power and admiration.
